kp.k: Harvey reports substantial improvement on its legal-task benchmark
kp.d: Harvey reports that base model scores on its own BigLaw Bench (BLB), published in 2024, rose from 60% for GPT 4o, Claude 3.5 and Gemini 1.5 to 90% for GPT-5, Claude 4.5 and Gemini 3. It associates this improvement with better recall, understanding and application of core legal principles. These are vendor-reported benchmark results, not reported measurements of workforce displacement or client outcomes.
qs: Over time, model performance has steadily improved on BLB with base model scores going from 60%** (GPT 4o | Claude 3.5 | Gemini 1.5) to **90%** (GPT-5 | Claude 4.5 | Gemini 3).
This growth has paralleled improvements in the models’ ability to recall, understand, and apply core legal principles to tasks.

kp.k: Expert-defined task performance guides legal AI development
kp.d: Harvey says it continues measuring task completion, sourcing, hallucinations and retrieval, but finds task-solving performance against expert-written criteria its most accurate capability measure. It reports that improvements usually correlate with its ability to deliver useful legal AI, and uses the benchmark to identify shortcomings, collaborate with foundation model labs and examine performance under different constraints.
qs: While we continue to measure all of these things, we have found that the most accurate measure of model capabilities is core BLB: **their ability to solve tasks as graded by objective, expert-written criteria**.
More often than not, as models improve on these tasks, they improve our ability to build and deliver valuable AI solutions to lawyers.

This correlation has allowed the Harvey team to understand where models may fall short of delivering value to lawyers; work with foundation model labs to improve model capabilities for law; and probe model capabilities to understand how they behave under different constraints.

kp.k: Legal distinctions expose model weaknesses and possible mitigations
kp.d: Harvey describes a US federal evidence task distinguishing admissible non-testimonial statements that are not hearsay from hearsay statements nonetheless admissible. Early models conflated or reversed the categories; Harvey says most now handle them correctly, especially with web search. It treats this task as a diagnostic prompting further investigation of other legal concepts, not proof of deficiencies across those concepts, and identifies better-aligned models and live data as possible mitigations.
qs: In early measures, many models failed this task by conflating which types of statements fell into each group or, worse, sometimes reversing the two groups entirely.
Nowadays, most models can iterate through these groups correctly — especially when provided access to web search to confirm their priors.
This single BLB task serves as a canary for collecting additional data on any model’s internalization of legal rules.
It also gives us the ability to mitigate this gap for our customers through the use of better aligned models or access to live data.

kp.k: Benchmark gaps can direct closer human scrutiny
kp.d: Harvey Applied Legal Researcher Laura Toulme argues that benchmark failures identify practice-relevant weaknesses and help lawyers recognize where closer scrutiny and human judgment matter most. This is an internal researcher's interpretation of the benchmark's usefulness, rather than a quantified finding about verification effort.
qs: Reviewing BLB benchmarks made it easier to see where models struggle in ways that matter for practice. Those gaps aren’t just technical issues, they’re signals that help lawyers know when closer scrutiny is needed and where human judgment adds the most value.

kp.k: Prompt framing tests reveal susceptibility to sycophancy
kp.d: Responding to concerns about sycophancy in 2025, Harvey tested tasks that appeared subjective but had expert-agreed answers. Its Most Favored Nations side-letter example used three framings: neutral, a general partner seeking a loophole and an MFN holder seeking the benefit. Harvey says these tests identified susceptible models and informed guardrails. Applied Legal Researcher Beth de la Roche emphasizes lawyers' evaluation of reasoning shifts; the article supplies no model-specific results or numerical effect sizes.
qs: In the side letter example, we posed the question three different ways: (1) neutrally, (2) as the general partner hoping to find a loophole, and (3) as the MFN holder hoping to obtain the proposed benefit.
In the latter two cases, we looked to whether the model swayed from an accurate prediction based on our stated interest in the result.
This helped us identify models prone to sycophancy and to build better guardrails against this behavior.
Having lawyers evaluate those shifts helped distinguish confident legal analysis from answers that were merely responsive to framing.

kp.k: Expansion prioritizes behavioral insights over definitive outcome predictions
kp.d: The February 2026 article announces an expansion intended to increase public BLB data points more than fivefold in the coming months across global law, practice areas and legal research. Harvey explicitly qualifies the benchmark as a means of understanding model behavior rather than obtaining answers about specific outcomes. Methodological deep dives and updated scores are forthcoming, not results presented here.
qs: In the coming months, we’ll be releasing extended benchmarks that increase the number of BLB data points more than fivefold.
This data reflects research in three key areas: **global law, practice areas, and legal research**.
While BLB is an incredibly powerful framework for understanding models, it is not yet a silver bullet.
As we set out to expand the benchmark, we wanted to focus where it had been most impactful — providing insights about model behavior rather than answers about specific outcomes.

kp.k: Global benchmarks test jurisdiction-specific legal capabilities
kp.d: Harvey situates its Global dataset within serving customers in more than 60 countries and offering more than 400 international data sources. Built with local experts, the dataset starts with the UK, Australia and Spain and is intended to test whether model capabilities translate to local law and distinctive jurisdictional problems. The article does not report comparative jurisdictional scores.
qs: Harvey now serves customers in more than 60 countries, with more than 400 international [data sources](/en-US/platform/knowledge) available and a commitment to further our [internationalization efforts](/en-US/blog/using-agents-to-scale-harveys-knowledge-sources).
Built in collaboration with local experts in each country, our Global dataset tests a model’s ability to solve local problems, starting with benchmarks for the UK, Australia, and Spain.

kp.k: Practice-area testing targets end-to-end task completion
kp.d: Harvey describes a practice-area expansion built by Applied Legal Researchers mapping core tasks and constructing datasets to test models' ability to understand, support and solve them. Initial coverage comprises Capital Markets, Mergers and Acquisitions, Fund Formation, Litigation, Arbitration and Intellectual Property. End-to-end completion is a testing focus, not a demonstrated claim that these practices can operate without lawyers.
qs: Where Global is focused on geographical breadth, Practice Areas focuses on depth and end-to-end task completion.
For each practice area, Harvey Applied Legal Researchers worked to map out core tasks and build datasets that tested models’ ability to understand, support, and solve those tasks.

kp.k: Research benchmarks examine search-enabled models and unresolved tasks
kp.d: The Legal Research extension targets model and agent search capabilities on complex research problems, beginning with US case law. Harvey aims both to track improvements and to identify problems models are currently poorly suited to solve, using benchmarking to develop strategies for more capable AI research rather than claiming that difficult legal research is already solved.
qs: Model and agent search capabilities on complex research problems
Legal Research focuses on a model’s cross-practice abilities to solve hard research problems when provided with search tools.
Our initial legal research dataset (US case law research) also focuses on identifying legal research problems that models are currently not well-suited to solve.
Here, the focus is not just tracking model improvements, but providing benchmarks for finding unique strategies to make models more capable researchers.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Harvey Team claims that improving models are better at solving legal tasks and enabling useful lawyer-facing AI; its expanded benchmark will investigate capabilities and remaining limitations across jurisdictions, practice areas, and research.
pts.d: The Harvey Team reports that base-model BigLaw Bench scores rose from 60% for GPT 4o, Claude 3.5, and Gemini 1.5 to 90% for GPT-5, Claude 4.5, and Gemini 3, alongside improved recall, understanding, and application of legal principles. It claims that task-based benchmarking helps Harvey identify capability gaps, improve models with foundation-model labs, and develop mitigations such as access to live data and guardrails against sycophancy. Its evidence-law example describes models becoming better at distinguishing closely related legal categories, particularly with web search. Harvey Applied Legal Researcher Laura Toulme says benchmark gaps indicate where lawyers need closer scrutiny and human judgment. Applied Legal Researcher Beth de la Roche says lawyer evaluation of reasoning under different framings helps distinguish legal analysis from answers that simply accommodate the prompt. The planned expansion is a claim about future measurement and development, not a finding that models can already complete all covered workflows or replace lawyers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of Harvey’s own benchmark results, illustrative task and prompt-framing tests, and observations by its applied legal researchers.
pts.d: BigLaw Bench is Harvey’s benchmark, not an independent vendor evaluation. The article reports aggregate base-model score improvement and identifies task grading against expert-written criteria as its preferred capability measure. It illustrates improvement through a US federal evidence-law task distinguishing admissible non-testimonial statements that are not hearsay from hearsay statements that are nevertheless admissible. It also describes testing sycophancy using a Most Favored Nations side-letter question posed neutrally and from two interested parties’ perspectives. Harvey says these tests informed guardrails, but the article supplies no numerical sycophancy results or quantified guardrail effects. The claimed connection between benchmark improvements and customer value is based on Harvey’s development experience; the article does not present measured client outcomes, productivity gains, or cost savings. The new datasets and scores are previewed rather than reported.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article distinguishes observed progress since BLB’s 2024 launch from planned 2026 expansion, and qualifies both model capability and what benchmark results establish.
pts.d: Published February 9, 2026, the article looks back to BLB’s 2024 introduction and sycophancy testing prompted by concerns in 2025. Methodological deep dives are promised beginning within the next few weeks, followed by updated scores for major models; extended benchmarks increasing data points more than fivefold are promised in the coming months. Initial jurisdictional coverage is the UK, Australia, and Spain; initial research coverage is US case law. Some task improvements depend particularly on web-search access, and the research benchmark explicitly tests models supplied with search tools. Harvey qualifies the benchmark as a source of insights into behavior rather than definitive answers about particular outcomes and acknowledges research tasks that models remain poorly suited to solve.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern lawyers using Harvey, international legal teams, specialist practitioners, and the researchers and model developers building their tools.
pts.d: Lawyers are described as benefiting from more capable AI tools and clearer signals about where closer human scrutiny remains necessary. Litigators are specifically exposed to errors in evidentiary distinctions. International customers are the intended beneficiaries of jurisdiction-specific testing developed with local experts, initially covering the UK, Australia, and Spain. Practice-area testing targets Capital Markets, Mergers and Acquisitions, Fund Formation, Litigation, Arbitration, and Intellectual Property, with an emphasis on support for core tasks and end-to-end completion. Legal researchers are affected by efforts to improve difficult search-enabled research, initially in US case law. Harvey’s team and foundation-model labs use benchmark insights to identify and address weaknesses. The article does not make substantive predictions about lawyer employment, staffing structures, billing models, or access to justice.
